notable.title: Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)
notable.description: The closest the two Cold War superpowers ever came to full-scale thermonuclear war. Following U-2 spy plane discovery of Soviet medium-range nuclear ballistic missile installations in Cuba, President Kennedy imposed a naval quarantine (technically a blockade, coded as Use of Force in COW) and issued an ultimatum for missile removal. Secret concessions included US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret reciprocal withdrawal of US Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

notable.title: The July Crisis & Outbreak of World War I (1914)
notable.description: Triggered by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip. Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia with German "blank check" backing. Russia mobilized to protect Serbia, causing German mobilization under the Schlieffen Plan and rapid invasion of Belgium, drawing the United Kingdom into a general European conflagration.

notable.title: Korean War (1950–1953)
notable.description: Kim Il Sung launched an invasion across the 38th parallel with Soviet authorization. The US mobilized UN authorization while the USSR was boycotting the Security Council. Following MacArthur's Inchon landing and advance to the Yalu River, China intervened with hundreds of thousands of troops. War ended in an enduring military armistice along the DMZ.

notable.title: Suez Crisis (1956)
notable.description: Following Gamal Abdel Nasser's nationalization of the Suez Canal Company, Britain, France, and Israel secretly conspired (Protocol of Sèvres) to invade Egypt. The United States under Eisenhower refused to support the operation and applied immense financial pressure on the British Pound, forcing an ignominious Anglo-French withdrawal and signaling the end of Britain and France as global imperial superpowers.

notable.title: Six-Day War (1967)
notable.description: Spurred by Soviet false intelligence of Israeli troop buildups, Egyptian expulsion of UNEF peacekeepers, and closure of the Straits of Tiran. Israel launched a decisive preemptive air strike on June 5, destroying the Egyptian Air Force on the tarmac and capturing the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights in six days.

notable.title: Yom Kippur War / October War (1973)
irConcepts: Coercive Bargaining to Force Peace Talks
notable.description: Egypt and Syria launched a surprise coordinated two-front offensive across the Suez Canal (Operation Badr) and Golan Heights during Yom Kippur to break diplomatic stalemate. After initial Arab advances, Israeli counter-offensives encircled Egypt's Third Army. Led directly to Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy and the 1978 Camp David Accords.

notable.title: Falklands / Malvinas War (1982)
notable.description: The Argentine military junta led by Gen. Leopoldo Galtieri invaded the British-held Falkland Islands to divert domestic public fury away from economic collapse and human rights abuses (Diversionary War). Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher dispatched a British naval task force 8,000 miles to retake the islands, leading to the collapse of the Argentine junta and restoration of democracy.

notable.title: Third Taiwan Strait Crisis (1995–1996)
notable.description: Triggered by Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui's visit to Cornell University. The PLA conducted missile tests, amphibious landing drills, and live-fire exercises in the waters off Keelung and Kaohsiung to intimidate voters before Taiwan's first direct democratic presidential election. President Clinton deployed two US aircraft carrier battle groups (USS Nimitz and USS Independence) to the strait in the largest US naval display in Asia since Vietnam.

notable.title: Kargil Conflict (1999)
notable.description: Pakistani troops and paramilitaries infiltrated across the Line of Control into fortified high-altitude positions in Indian-controlled Kargil, Kashmir. Marked the first direct military conflict between India and Pakistan after both officially conducted nuclear tests in 1998, illustrating Glenn Snyder's Stability-Instability Paradox: strategic nuclear parity created a protective umbrella under which lower-level conventional aggression was attempted.

notable.title: Russo-Georgian War (2008)
notable.description: Following Georgian shelling and advance into Tskhinvali to reassert control over separatist South Ossetia, Russia launched a massive counter-offensive through the Roki Tunnel, driving deep into uncontested Georgian territory and bombing Gori and Poti. Russia subsequently recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states, effectively foreclosing Georgia's immediate path into NATO.

notable.title: Crimea Annexation & War in Donbas (2014)
notable.description: Following Ukraine's Euromaidan Revolution and the ouster of President Viktor Yanukovych, Russian special forces without insignias ("little green men") seized the Crimean parliament and military bases. A disputed referendum was staged, leading to Russia's formal annexation of Crimea and the ignition of armed conflict in the Donbas (Donetsk and Luhansk), shattering post-Cold War European security architecture.

notable.title: Fashoda Incident (1898)
notable.description: Climax of imperial territorial disputes between Britain (seeking a continuous north-south Cape-to-Cairo axis) and France (seeking a west-to-east Dakar-to-Djibouti axis). The forces of Capt. Marchand and Gen. Kitchener met at Fashoda on the White Nile. Recognizing British naval superiority and growing German danger in Europe, France yielded, paving the way for the 1904 Entente Cordiale.
